correctness.rationale: A graph vertex has a singleton lower set and a graph edge has a three-point lower set. For a vertex root, all other vertices enter at 1 and its incident edges enter at 2, joining exactly d_v isolated vertices to the root component without a cycle. For an edge root the two endpoints with the subdividing point already form a connected path at 0; the other vertices enter at 1. The level-2 double star joins k_e distinct outside vertices, and after taking its root edge and one edge per outside vertex as a tree, the remaining edges are precisely one per common neighbor. This proves the c_e cycle births at 2. All remaining edges enter at 3; graph inclusions inject cycle spaces and introduce nothing in higher dimension, and the full subdivision is connected with cycle rank m-n+1. This gives the claimed ordinary barcodes, also for a single edge, with triangle recovery by summing c_e and dividing by three. Petersen and the pentagonal prism have the same substituted profiles. They differ by existence of a four-cycle; both incidence posets have no beat points and are their own Stong cores. The finite-space nonhomotopy is not a claim of distinct order-complex weak types. Fresh replay on 771 connected labelled graphs (8100 roots) through five vertices and the named pair corroborates these deductions.
residual_risks: Replay is finite and independent of the uploaded checker. The proof applies only to the specified lower-topology order-complex filtration of connected simple graphs and the nonhomotopy statement uses ordinary finite-space homotopy.

value.rationale: For a basic family of finite spaces this gives an exact interpretation of what the established filtration sees: all rooted intervals have a simple combinatorial origin, and a degree-one edge-root birth counts local triangles. The named pair shows the complete root-tagged invariant cannot determine the ordinary finite-space core, despite detecting these graph features. That joint classification and limitation is useful beyond a small computation or the known complete-graph substitution.
